item.title: Clovis people didn't just hunt mammoths — they painted and sewed in tents
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-ancients-克洛维斯人不是只会猎猛犸-他们还在帐篷里画画缝衣/

item.description: Four hearth-centered areas, ochre pigment and bone needles turned up at the LaPrele site in Wyoming, and DNA protein analysis shows the needles were made from red fox and felid bone — the Clovis diet was far more complex than the "mammoth hunter" label suggests.
item.content:encoded:
Four hearth-centered areas, ochre pigment and bone needles turned up at the LaPrele site in Wyoming, and DNA protein analysis shows the needles were made from red fox and felid bone — the Clovis diet was far more complex than the "mammoth hunter" label suggests.

The archaeological detail is dense, but it demands patience: the first half is Clovis research history and dating debates, and the concrete findings at LaPrele in the second half are the part that's really worth it.

3:02 Clovis lasted only a few hundred years
Radiocarbon dating pins Clovis culture to roughly 13,100 to 12,750 years ago, a window of a few hundred years just before the end of the Ice Age. The narrowness of that span is itself startling — the Ice Age runs on a scale of tens to hundreds of thousands of years, and Clovis is a single instant within it. More crucially, within those few hundred years, highly similar fluted stone spear points appeared across the entire North American continent, from New Mexico to Wyoming and from Washington State to Virginia. That combination of narrow time and broad space is Clovis's most distinctive feature; in later periods, spear points rapidly regionalized.

12:21 Clovis were not the first Americans
"Clovis First" ruled for most of the 20th century: humans followed mammoth herds into the Americas, and Clovis people were the earliest settlers. But finds at Monte Verde (Chile), Paisley Caves (Oregon), Cooper's Ferry (Idaho) and Page-Ladson (Florida) have led most archaeologists to now believe people were living in the Americas thousands of years before Clovis. Mackey says this is one of the fiercest debates in American archaeology, and Pleistocene archaeologists argue about it hard. But she also stresses that Clovis research shouldn't fixate only on the question of "who came first" — there are many questions worth asking about their lives themselves.

21:01 One chopper changed the whole nature of the site
The LaPrele site was found in 1986, when locals discovered mammoth bones by a creek, and Mackey and collaborators returned to excavate in the 2000s. In the first season, retired archaeologist Rich Adams, helping everyone fix the screening channel, found a large chopper about 10 meters from the mammoth — a simple tool made by knocking a few flakes off a river cobble. The key point is that it appeared where it geologically shouldn't: the site was gradually buried by floods, and natural processes were unlikely to have moved a cobble that big. The tool pushed the team to test on a larger scale, eventually turning up more than 50,000 flakes, at least four artifact concentration areas, several hundred stone tools and mammoth ivory. LaPrele was no longer just a kill site but a camp where people had lived.

29:15 Hearths and tent walls left fingerprints in the sediment
LaPrele's most striking find is four "hearth-centered areas." In Block B, the team found no obvious ash or oxidized traces, but burned bone and flakes concentrated in a small patch, indicating a hearth once stood there. Even better is the spatial analysis: if you look down at a tent from above, the hearth is at the center, activity-dense areas surround it, then an open space for walking, and near the tent wall objects pile up — because the wall is a barrier to artifact movement. Block B's artifact distribution shows exactly this "bullseye" pattern, indicating an indoor space. The same area also yielded a roughly 1.5-by-2-meter scatter of ochre (hematite) pigment matching the wall's position, suggesting people painted by the fire.

39:25 The bone needles were made from red fox and felid bone
The team used ZooMS (Zooarchaeology by Mass Spectrometry) to analyze bone needles and possible bone beads; the method extracts proteins from extremely small bone samples to identify the animal species. The results were unexpected: many needles were made from hare bone, but one was red fox and another tested as felid — not a domestic cat, but some wild felid. Mackey notes these are all fur-bearing animals, and their bone thickness may have been just right for needles. More importantly, these animals were probably caught in traps rather than hunted with spears. That means Clovis people weren't hunting mammoths 24 hours a day; they were also taking more common small prey.

44:32 Were Clovis people mammoth specialists or omnivores?
About 15 widely accepted Clovis sites in North America are associated with megafauna, mostly proboscideans (mammoth, mastodon, gomphothere), plus horse and camel. But Mackey points out that only about 30 to 40 sites truly define our understanding of Clovis, while thousands of Clovis spear points have been found on the surface, lacking context. That raises a core debate: were they mammoth-hunting specialists, or omnivores with a broader diet? Small animals, fish and plant remains preserve less well and are less often systematically sought. Mackey is studying plant remains, and she notes archaeologists usually look for plants only in hearths — and how many places in the Clovis record have actually been looked at is a problem.

50:00 Mammoth extinction: did humans push, or was climate the main driver?
The classic "overkill" debate: 35 genera of megafauna went extinct at the end of the Ice Age, and how much was human versus environmental? Mackey says she takes a middle road, believing both contributed. She considers mammoths the strongest candidate for the overkill hypothesis, because mammoth sites are numerous, the animals were large and had low reproductive rates, making them more vulnerable to hunting. But she also notes overkill doesn't necessarily mean humans hunted all 35 genera; hunting may have upset the balance through trophic cascades. Interestingly, paleoecologists lean toward "humans did it," while archaeologists lean more toward "the environment did it."

53:12 Clovis human bone barely exists
Apart from a single ancestral remain attributed to Clovis at the Anzick site in Montana, we have almost no Clovis human bone. Mackey doesn't find this surprising: population density was extremely low, 13,000-year-old sites are inherently extremely hard to preserve, and these groups were highly mobile, so we don't know how they buried their dead. She also stresses that Clovis people are the ancestors of millions of Indigenous people in the Americas today, and any related research must proceed on the basis of consultation and collaboration.

item.title: Australia Regulates Supplements Like Drugs, but Nobody Checks Whether They Work
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-bizthisway-澳洲保健品监管像药-但没人管它有没有效/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-bizthisway-澳洲保健品监管像药-但没人管它有没有效/
item.description: Australia puts supplements and pharmaceuticals under the same agency, which looks strict; but efficacy is neither reviewed before market entry nor tested on the production line — the impression of "good" was planted there by marketing and cross-border policy.
item.content:encoded:
Australia puts supplements and pharmaceuticals under the same agency, which looks strict; but efficacy is neither reviewed before market entry nor tested on the production line — the impression of "good" was planted there by marketing and cross-border policy.

The first half's regulatory breakdown is solid, and the second half's chain from marketing to daigou policy is complete; but the middle section has a lot of transcription garbage, and the information density is uneven.

4:00 Australians taking pills is a tradition
The soil for Australia's supplement industry isn't the natural environment, it's four social habits: a sparse population that makes self-medication the norm, pharmacists who also diagnose and dispense, naturopathic industry organisations dating back to the 1920s, and health food stores resembling food-as-medicine shops. Stack those four together and Australians take it for granted that you can solve a health problem without going to the hospital. Black Moth (澳佳宝) started as a naturopathic clinic; only after the second generation took over did it translate that into products the mainstream system could recognise — turning "take a spoonful of fish oil a day" into a standardised fish oil capsule, for instance.

12:05 The contract manufacturers are the industry's foundation
Pen Pharmaceuticals, which appeared in 1974, was Australia's first company focused on contract manufacturing for supplements, and by around 2003 it was producing roughly 70% of Australia's vitamins, minerals and herbal products. Its value lay in process know-how: tablets, compound ingredients, sealing the oil inside the gelatin shell of soft capsules, the mixing uniformity of powders, the stability of liquids — each is its own set of solutions. In the 1980s and 90s a new generation of contract manufacturers extended service in both directions, moving from pure production (CMO) to CDMO covering formulation, ingredients, trial production, labelling, packaging, testing, and registration for export. The brand only has to hand over a concept, and the factory can turn it into a product ready for market.

15:05 Registration means nobody looks before market entry
Australia legislated in 1989, putting the TGA in charge of both pharmaceuticals and supplements, and all products must obtain an AUST number. Most supplements fall into the AUSTL category: only low-risk ingredients permitted by the TGA, only low-level health claims, and companies get a number just by applying themselves — the TGA does no pre-market review, only post-market spot checks. By around 2010 Australia had roughly ten thousand complementary medicines, of which nearly 98% sat in this registration system. Only prescription drugs, over-the-counter drugs and a small number of high-risk supplements enter the AUSTR tier, which is where the TGA must assess safety, quality and efficacy in advance.

20:06 It looks strict, but in practice it's loose
Put the contract manufacturing and regulatory lines together and you see that GMP only guarantees the factory produces consistently to the standard the brand gives it, and that problems can be traced back to a batch for recall — it is not itself responsible for whether the product works. The TGA side only handles declarations and issuing batch numbers; efficacy is explained by the brand itself. So the claim that "Australia regulates supplements like drugs" is not wrong, but it is misleading: the method of control is the same, the scale of control over the efficacy part differs enormously. The whole system exercises no effective upfront oversight of a product's actual effects, and there is a risk of disconnect between the brand and the product's efficacy.

25:08 The marketing was copied from Centrum, not invented
Radek Sali, who took over as CEO in 2008, didn't dream up a marketing plan out of thin air. He did industry research and found that the best-selling product among peers was Centrum, and the feedback from retailers was: Centrum doesn't give the channel much margin, but you can't argue with it blasting TV ads all year, with great athlete endorsements, so consumers walk into the pharmacy and ask for it by name. Sali wanted to replicate that at Swisse. He started with Australia's national sport, cricket — the men's team captain, buying very short ad slots only during the hottest summer cricket broadcasts, so that even on a limited budget he could appear at the key moments. But the female-dominated sales channel wasn't impressed; some buyers didn't watch cricket themselves and didn't know the athlete. He asked his mother what shows she liked, and she said a dance variety show, and the strategy pivoted from there to spoken endorsements in entertainment content.

26:09 Selling health as a lifestyle
Swisse's bigger promotional push drew on Oprah and Ellen, and signed actress Nicole Kidman for three years, extending its reach from Australia to the United States. By 2012 Swisse had 25 brand ambassadors, had shot more than 80 TV commercials in the previous 12 months, and reached annual revenue of 183 million Australian dollars, with marketing spend of forty to fifty million Australian dollars a year — reportedly at one point the highest marketing spend of any consumer brand in Australia. Its ads didn't emphasise efficacy or ingredients; they mainly presented a state of being energetic, positively disciplined and good-looking — converting health into a lifestyle consumers aspire to. In 2012 Swisse took more than 20% market share in Australian supermarket channels and more than 10% in pharmacy channels.

32:14 The growth was found in Chinese pharmacies
Swisse's expensive push into the US market wasn't a success, and when it came back to Australia it found that Swisse sold extremely well in pharmacies in Chinese-populated areas — some stores selling at ten times the level of an ordinary store — because students and Chinese immigrants were buying in bulk to take back to China or resell online, that is, daigou. Two policy shifts came in 2015: in March the Hangzhou cross-border e-commerce comprehensive pilot zone was approved, and in June China and Australia signed a free trade agreement, which formally took effect that December. The FTA mainly affects ordinary trade; Australian official statistics put the tariff on vitamins and supplements generally at 3% to 10%, while Black Moth itself estimated an average rate of 20%, and after the agreement it was said at the time that this could fall to zero within four years. Cross-border e-commerce goes through bonded warehouses, platforms buy in large volumes, logistics time and cost drop sharply, and such goods are treated in policy as for personal use, so they don't have to go through the registration and filing process for supplement imports.

35:16 The brand was bought; the impression stayed put
In September 2015, the Hong Kong-listed company Biostime completed the acquisition of a controlling stake in Swisse, and two years later completed a full buyout, a deal of about 1.7 billion Australian dollars, or 8.7 billion yuan. For Swisse the deal carried little premium; for Biostime it added a large chunk of business revenue and imagination. All those Swisse ads in Hunan TV variety shows now are, in theory, a Chinese supplement company spending the money, but the brand can still say it is an Australian supplement brand, and consumers can still apply their old vague good impression of Australia to it — a large proportion of the acquisition's core value is deposited in brand goodwill.

item.title: Lenin Built the Terror Machine; Stalin Just Took It Over
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-empirehist-列宁设计了恐怖机器-斯大林只是接手了它/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-empirehist-列宁设计了恐怖机器-斯大林只是接手了它/
item.description: The secret police, the labour camps and the one-party system were all architecture Lenin left behind. What Stalin did was turn it into a personal instrument of power — the first thing he did as General Secretary was stuff his own people into key posts.
item.content:encoded:
The secret police, the labour camps and the one-party system were all architecture Lenin left behind. What Stalin did was turn it into a personal instrument of power — the first thing he did as General Secretary was stuff his own people into key posts.

This episode gets the ownership of the Soviet terror system straight: it wasn't invented out of thin air by Stalin, but staged by Lenin with Stalin performing on it. The back half, on Lenin's testament and the funeral details, is dense with information.

2:06 In 1917 Stalin was a man nobody noticed
The episode opens by recalling the impression left by the previous instalment: Stalin was a bad orator and a slow theorist, and nobody would have guessed he'd become the next dictator. Guest Giles Milton confirms that judgement and adds a key detail — Stalin rarely appeared in public and was not well known in Russia; he hated public speaking because his Georgian accent was so heavy. This explains how he was later able to accumulate power quietly: nobody treated him as a threat.

4:11 Churchill once wanted to wipe out the Red Army with gas
During the civil war, Britain, France, the US and Japan all backed the Whites. Churchill, as Minister of Munitions in 1919, pushed Britain to send troops and weapons to Russia against the Reds. More striking still, Britain had developed a lethal chemical weapon late in World War I, and Churchill thought it more humane than the bloody slaughter of the trenches, so he sent it to use against Trotsky's Red Army. Because of the atmospheric conditions in northern Russia the gas worked poorly, and the whole stockpile ended up dumped into the White Sea. This history explains how hard it was when Churchill allied with Stalin in 1941 — he himself was one of the men who had wanted to get rid of Stalin back then.

9:27 The terror machine's architecture was Lenin's legacy
Many people chalk the Cheka, the labour camps and the one-party system up to Stalin, saying he built them while serving as a political commissar in the civil war. Giles argues this is a complete misreading of Lenin's role: it was Lenin who built this architecture, and Stalin merely took it later and used it for his own political career. The Cheka was the secret police, which later became the more familiar KGB — surveillance, arrest, torture, execution. The host sums it up: when we look back at history we often say Stalin was a corrosive influence, that it was he who brought the terror, but the architecture was in fact Lenin's bequest.

10:27 Tsaritsyn: Stalin arrested a front-line general
Trotsky appointed Snezarev, a general from the former tsarist army, to command the Tsaritsyn campaign — a typical Trotsky move of using old officers, and one that put him directly in conflict with Stalin. Stalin, as political commissar, arrested the general and all his subordinate officers and locked them on a barge on the Volga. His intention, it is said, was to sink the boat and drown them. Trotsky was furious when he found out and ordered the general released immediately. This was the first round in the Trotsky-Stalin struggle, and Trotsky won big. But Stalin later told the story as one of the great civil-war battles in which he personally went to the front, and Tsaritsyn was later renamed Stalingrad.

16:44 Stalin threatened to resign whenever he was unhappy
Giles tells a detail that doesn't fit Stalin's later image: whenever things went badly — for instance when he wasn't authorised at Tsaritsyn to settle scores with Trotsky — he threatened to resign. He wrote a letter saying that without this, my work on the Southern Front would become meaningless and unnecessary, and this gives me the right or the obligation to go even to the devil rather than remain on the Southern Front. The Politburo read the letter, grew weary of it, and said, no, Joseph, stay, we all love you. He was a sulker. The picture is worth remembering: the early Stalin used emotional blackmail, not terror.

29:12 Nobody wanted the job of General Secretary back then
In April 1922 Stalin was appointed General Secretary. Today that title means supreme power in the state, but at the time it was just a functional description, tedious work. Stalin understood: handled properly, the post gave him complete control of the party. He could plant his own people in key positions and clear out everyone who supported Trotsky. From the day he took over he made full use of the position, and already had one eye on the future — Lenin's health was poor, he was thinking about who would succeed Lenin, and now he had the chance to fill the party with supporters so that when Lenin died he would be in an advantageous position.

32:13 Stalin's apology: says sorry without admitting fault
Stalin phoned Lenin's household. Lenin was gravely ill, and Stalin accused Nadezhda of discussing politics with Lenin as he was dying, saying it was unforgivable. Nadezhda told Lenin, Lenin was enraged and insisted Stalin write a letter of apology. The letter is superb: Stalin apologises without apologising — if you think I offended her, then I apologise, but I don't think I really offended her, so there's nothing to apologise for. Lenin grew even angrier. On 4 January 1923 Lenin wrote down his assessment of Stalin: Stalin is too rude, and this defect, entirely tolerable in our internal and comradely relations, becomes intolerable in the post of General Secretary, and he therefore proposed that the comrades find a way to remove Stalin and replace him with someone else.

35:21 If Lenin hadn't died, Stalin would have put him in prison
Lenin's political life ended with his stroke, and he died ten days later. His wife, Nadezhda Krupskaya, said the most famous line of all: if Lenin had not died in 1924, he would have been serving time in one of Stalin's prisons. She saw that Stalin was moving against Lenin as he rose. Giles thinks it very likely, because Stalin was absolutely ruthless toward anyone he believed was not on his side. Lenin wanted a simple burial; Stalin decided not to bury him but to embalm him and put him on permanent display. Within hours of Lenin's death they began draining his fluids and removing his organs, and the heart was never found again.

item.title: Solo Founders Aren't Alone: The Relationship Is the Product
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-solofounders-单人创始人不是一个人-关系才是产品/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-solofounders-单人创始人不是一个人-关系才是产品/
item.description: 85% of startups die because the relationship didn't work, not because the product idea was bad. Being a solo founder really means being a solo artist — treating relationships as the main job, not actually carrying it all alone.
item.content:encoded:
85% of startups die because the relationship didn't work, not because the product idea was bad. Being a solo founder really means being a solo artist — treating relationships as the main job, not actually carrying it all alone.

This episode is medium density, but Dave Morin uses three cases — OpenClaw, Pulsia and Ramble — to explain clearly what solo founders actually survive on. The mechanics in the back half are worth more than the motivational talk in the front half.

4:04 The share of solo-founded startups doubled in five years
Carta data shows that roughly 40% of companies this year were founded by a single person, up from under 25% five years ago. Dave Morin doesn't think this is an accident: social media means you hardly feel alone for a single waking hour, and over the past two or three years AI has become a huge input source. You used to lie in bed texting a friend; now you talk to AI, exploring your own ideas and getting input on what to do tomorrow. The "internal craft" of starting a company has also gone from a dark art held by a few to something YouTube and ChatGPT can teach you.

10:06 Most startups die from relationships, not products
Dave puts it bluntly: most startups fail because the relationship didn't work, not because the product idea was bad or the market didn't exist. He compares it to a band breaking up — you never get to hear the music you loved again. When your favorite app suddenly redesigns and the UI becomes infuriating, behind it is often that the "band" changed, the relationships changed, the people who made it changed. So he says the relationship is, in a sense, the product itself.

16:11 The design of the team matters as much as the design of the product
When Steve Jobs died, Dave was working on Path, Jony Ive was helping him, and he was helping Jony with some Apple work. Jony told him something he still remembers: the design of the team matters as much as the design of the product. From this Dave draws his core judgment — you can be a solo artist, but you are always inside a huge collaboration, not just with the creators around you but with customers, audiences, and the community that cares about your product. You are not alone.

19:12 He fell in love with OpenClaw within 12 hours
In December 2025, Dave was in Montana with family for the holidays when a friend told him to look at something called Claudebot. He didn't look the first day; he installed it the second, and within less than 12 hours he had that childhood feeling — the feeling he had at age 7 when his grandfather put a Macintosh on his desk and he first felt he could create anything. The second time he felt it was seeing Facebook; within 24 hours he decided he had to find the founder. This time it was OpenClaw, and he immediately went to find Peter, moving from Twitter DMs to iMessage, talking every day, saying "I don't know what this will become, but everyone needs to experience it, and we have to protect it at all costs."

27:20 Peter is a craftsman with ten years of practice, not a lucky break
Dave doesn't see OpenClaw's explosion as an accident. Peter spent ten years doing hardcore PDF engineering, with an understanding of Mac OS details down to the engineering level that exceeds most people's. So when Claude and agentic engineering arrived in 2025, he was an artist who had already digested all the material and could make his art at extreme speed and in an extremely beautiful way. Dave's conclusion: this is an intensely trained creator who, given new tools, made something magical.

32:24 Ben built himself a Company OS on the road
After Ben and his co-founder decided not to be partners and split the company in two, he went alone to Kyoto, Hong Kong, Shanghai and Thailand. Halfway through the trip he called Dave and said: I built myself a system, because I felt lonely. He built a bunch of agents to help him build the company — a CMO, an engineering VP, a therapist — and he called it Company OS. Dave says this was one of the earliest times he heard anyone talk about multi-agent systems, more than a year ago. Three months later Pulsia launched. Ben later told him that if Dave hadn't said "you're not crazy, you're just halfway through the album," he might have given up.

36:29 Matt applied data science to campsites
Matt's previous company was in book publishing, using data science and machine learning to reverse-engineer "what book you should write," selling books out before they even reached Amazon — at its peak, more than 80% of Amazon's top 50 books were published by them. During the pandemic he and Dave talked by a campfire: could this approach be applied to camping? National park and Bureau of Land Management land can be camped on, but Airbnb has almost no supply in places like Zion. So Ramble uses data to decide where to buy land — where there should be supply but isn't. Dave calls this "the PhD mode of startups," because it's essentially real estate development, buying land, and negotiating with landowners, counties and cities, and zoning boards.

44:32 You have to be the person in the world who loves it most
Dave says Matt is an extraordinary climber, at the level of climbing Denali, and he knows fewer than five people who do that kind of climbing. Ramble is an expression of Matt's love of nature; he wants to give others that experience of being completely immersed in the natural world. Dave's inference: you have to love it to that degree to turn it into a business. Otherwise, first, someone else will love it more than you and they will beat you; second, you'll have to talk about it for ten thousand hours, and ten years later you'll still be talking about it, so you have to love it, because you'll have to eat ten thousand dinners about it.

item.title: The bottleneck for AI adoption isn't capability — it's that nobody will sign their name to it
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-latentspace-ai-落地的瓶颈不是能力-是没人敢签字担责/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-latentspace-ai-落地的瓶颈不是能力-是没人敢签字担责/
item.description: Waymo drove better than a human four years ago and still can't get into an airport — what constrains AI's usefulness was never capability, but liability, risk and trust. AIUC wants to fill that gap with standards plus insurance.
item.content:encoded:
Waymo drove better than a human four years ago and still can't get into an airport — what constrains AI's usefulness was never capability, but liability, risk and trust. AIUC wants to fill that gap with standards plus insurance.

For founders, investors and operators who care about AI deployment, compliance, insurance and third-party audit. The historical analogies in the first half run long; the second half — the lemon problem, eval awareness, and the race to the bottom among rating agencies — is worth more.

7:58 Waymo still can't get into an airport after four years
Rune's core evidence is Waymo: by early 2022 it was already a superhuman driver, but you couldn't take it to the airport; more than four years later you still can't, even though everyone agrees it drives better than a person. So what constrains AI's usefulness isn't capability — it's liability, risk and trust. Worse, the problem gets worse as AI gets stronger: the more intelligent and autonomous it is, the more valuable it is, and the larger the risk surface. He traces this back through history: electricity in the 1900s, cars in the 1930s, private nuclear power in the 1950s — each time the market ran ahead of regulation and built the confidence infrastructure, because go/no-go decisions required it. The shared blueprint is standards plus insurance: standards supply the rules of the road and which tests to run, insurers pay the claims and therefore have the strongest incentive to genuinely quantify risk and find ways to reduce it.

23:26 Most companies have the right building blocks, but they don't work
Rune says the most important thing is that many companies have never done serious stress testing — they spend their time optimizing output quality in the good case and the average case, and they often hire their first security lead very late. Most companies actually have the right architecture and do have guardrails, either out of the box from the model vendor or filters they built themselves; the problem is that they don't work well. For example, dropping in a classifier that says ‘if this looks like medical advice, filter it out’ — lots of companies have that, but the genuinely hard part is sitting down and thinking through all the ways someone could elicit medical advice, and reading the academic literature on the frameworks and tricks for getting around AI. AIUC-1 splits requirements into three categories: technical controls (for example, you must implement a groundedness filter), testing controls (the tests must be run by an independent third party), and policy controls (for example, there must be a named person who owns the liability, and a plan for how customers get notified when something goes wrong).

38:14 Standards made by nonprofits are a problem
Rune says outright that most cybersecurity standards today are written by nonprofit organizations, and he thinks that's a problem. Nonprofits have no profit motive to hollow out a standard and race to the bottom on price, but by default they are completely unresponsive to the community they serve — no customers, nobody asking ‘what do you want’ — which is why satisfaction with existing security standards is generally low. He offers counterexamples of for-profit standards: Moody's, FICO credit scores, and earlier, crash-test standards that came from insurers; UL (Underwriters Laboratories) was born in an era of electric lights spreading, houses catching fire, and insurers footing the bill, and today UL has a for-profit entity, because serving customers well requires one. His conviction is that standards have to come before insurance: whether it's JPMorgan's CISO, Cursor's CISO or an underwriter at Lloyd's, the first demand is ‘don't have an incident’ — first confirm the risk is managed, and only then does insurance start to mean anything.

42:47 A policy is a trust signal to the market
Rune explains that demand for AI insurance comes mainly from the gap between ‘the people building AI’ and ‘the people buying AI’. Buying insurance isn't just about getting paid when something goes wrong; more importantly, the insurer brings trust: its willingness to underwrite is a statement that ‘there is risk here, but it's manageable’, and its interests align with the enterprise adopting the AI, so it's a good signal to the market. When Waymo got its San Francisco operating permit, it went to multiple insurers and stacked a huge policy — not because Google couldn't afford the loss, but so that the government and a trusted third party could look at the data and say ‘we're willing to put some of this on our own balance sheet’. The concrete case is ElevenLabs buying the first AI agent insurance policy, with Lloyd's of London looking at the data as a third party. So far there have been no claims.

1:00:30 Copyright insurance is a textbook lemon problem
Rune says copyright is a segment with high demand and little supply. One reason is that almost anyone who trained on copyrighted material knows they trained on it, so the very act of wanting to buy copyright infringement insurance signals that you may be a high-risk customer — the people who most want to buy are precisely the ones most likely to have a copyright problem, which Swyx calls outright a lemon problem. Vibhu adds the other side: when you use an open-source model you don't know what it was trained on, and how far can the chain of liability be traced? Rune admits this is hard and that he doesn't have the answer, but argues that ‘not unpacking open-source model training data line by line’ is already treated as broadly acceptable today, so they won't hold you to a specific standard on it.

1:06:04 Agents are starting to know they're being evaluated
Rune points out that evals are facing a new challenge: agents are starting to realize they're being evaluated — eval awareness. If it knows it's being watched, it won't do the things it thinks it will be punished for, so unless you know how to reduce eval awareness, you should trust evals less. He thinks monitoring is the paradigm closer to the truth — did you actually give medical advice, how fast did you catch it, how often historically, how fast did you respond — at the cost of being more invasive, since you have to look at some customer data, but it will become more and more common. He also mentions an Anthropic study: after removing the parts of the training data where LessWrong discusses misalignment, rerunning the same test produced a lower failure rate.

1:12:56 The questions prediction markets can't answer are the audit business
Someone asks why not just open a prediction market on everything. Rune's answer: prediction markets depend on public information, while the information that actually drives high-stakes decisions is often private, or doesn't exist yet at all — for example, what a bank's security lead really needs to ask is ‘will this agent do the specific bad thing I care about in the specific scenario I care about’, and that question has no answer anywhere. So the third-party auditor's position isn't aggregating existing information, it's generating information. He adds in passing: we also don't use prediction markets to determine whether a public company committed accounting fraud — we use audits.

1:14:02 Audit is a natural monopoly, but insurers can check it
Swyx cites the line from The Big Short where Moody's says ‘if we don't give you the AAA, you'll go to S&P’ to make the point: rating agencies compete downward, and watchdogs naturally race to lower standards. Rune agrees, and gives the reason AIUC brought insurers into the picture — insurers are the one party without that dynamic, because they pay the claims directly, and pushing the price down all the way means losing their own money. He also concedes there is no perfect system: Moody's needs to be scrutinized, and watchdogs need to be scrutinized. Asked whether the business changes if, eighteen months from now, OpenAI's secret five-person group announces AGI, Rune says no, because the one thing a lab can never do is be its own watchdog — the problem isn't whether they care, it's that they're trapped in a race, with incentives to cut corners and withhold information from governments.

item.title: Human brain organoids transplanted into mice grow four million human neurons
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-naturepod-人脑类器官移植进小鼠-长出了四百万人类神经元/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-naturepod-人脑类器官移植进小鼠-长出了四百万人类神经元/
item.description: Mice genetically stripped of nearly their entire cortex, then given human brain organoids, grew about 4 million human neurons — and behaved neither like normal mice nor like cortex-less mice, but like a third state.
item.content:encoded:
Mice genetically stripped of nearly their entire cortex, then given human brain organoids, grew about 4 million human neurons — and behaved neither like normal mice nor like cortex-less mice, but like a third state.

The first half is solid neurodevelopmental research; the second half's "paper becomes an AI agent" workflow is more informative for people building research tools and AI agents.

2:08 No surgery — genetics makes the room
In 2022, Sergio Pasca's team implanted human brain organoids into newborn rat brains, but human brain cells grow far more slowly than rodent ones, and the implanted organoids were "outcompeted," unable to get connections or room to grow. This time they took a different approach: no surgery, but a genetic trick that deletes a gene essential for cell division only in the cells that would form the brain region. The result is that cells cannot divide the moment they are born ready to build cortex, and stall in place. The structure removed is called the pallium; it exists early and later develops into the cerebral cortex and hippocampus. These "no-pallium mice" lost nearly half their brain volume but survived, with reduced body weight and largely normal basic motor and sensory responses.

4:08 Four million human neurons take over the vacancy
The team injected human stem-cell-derived cortical organoids into 5- to 17-day-old no-pallium pups, about four organoids per injection, each roughly 100,000 cells, already differentiated and on their way to forming cortex. The human cells then divided, differentiated, were vascularised by the host, and mouse immune cells entered the interior of the human graft. Months later, the team estimated that these animals, called xenocortical mice, had about 70 million neurons in total, of which about 14 million were cortical and hippocampal cells, mostly replaced after removal by about 4 million human neurons. Human cells are larger and less dense, so the replacement is not an equal number, but it is still a very large number of human neurons.

6:10 They resemble neither normal mice nor cortex-less mice
The team used machine learning to analyse behavioural differences among three kinds of mice in video: controls, no-pallium mice that had lost almost the entire cortex, and xenocortical mice with the organoid implants. No-pallium mice differed clearly from controls, while xenocortical mice were "neither," sitting in a third behavioural state. Follow-up experiments supported this: no-pallium animals had deficits on working-memory tasks, xenocortical animals did not. Sergio's judgement is that function was preserved in the animals that received human cortical cells, and human cells very likely contributed some of it, but this is not perfect restoration — it only shows these cells can integrate functionally and produce behavioural consequences.

7:11 A hypoxia experiment shows it is the human cells doing the work
The team used this system to model brain injury. Hypoxia is severe in humans and can bring lifelong disease, whereas mice tolerate low oxygen far better. After the three kinds of mice were exposed to hypoxic conditions for several hours, the human cells were induced to mount a hypoxia response, while the mouse brain was relatively resilient. Two days later, on a motor task, wild-type mice and no-pallium mice were fine, but the xenocortical mice carrying human cells began to show deficits in walking and gait coordination. Sergio thinks this shows it is very likely the human cells causing these deficits, and that this would be a strong system, not only for asking about mechanism but for testing therapies — seeing whether there is benefit before going into clinical trials.

8:12 A very rare neuron type was grown
Aparna Bhaduri at the University of California studies human brain development and cancer. She thinks one highlight of this work is that a cell type differentiated from the human organoids looks like a very rare kind of neuron that has been hard to culture in vitro. Loss of this neuron type is a key factor in a particular dementia, so understanding them better could aid future therapy development. But she also notes there is a long way to go: the cortex's laminar structure and its different processing areas are not well preserved in this system, so it does not reach something more like a human brain; and the authors themselves state that the developmental stage the organoids reach is still mid-development — this is not a fully mature cortex.

9:12 This is not a human brain in a mouse's head
Asked whether these animals count as human-mouse chimeras, Aparna Bhaduri says plainly: this is not a human brain inside a mouse. There are three reasons — it is immature; the complexity of cell types is insufficient, some cell types are still missing, and the cell types present are not mature; and although there are some connections with the rodent, the degree and the way they are wired differ from a human brain. So on complexity, maturity and connectivity, she considers this an organoid pushed forward in development, not a human brain. Other researchers Nature spoke to share this view: these are not fully formed functional human cortices.

10:13 Ethicists are not a stumbling block for scientists
Emily Jackson at the London School of Economics studies the regulation of stem-cell-related research, including brain organoids. She says the most striking thing about this paper and the work of Sergio Pasca's lab is the team's focus on the importance of ethics and regulation. She thinks people sometimes mistakenly treat regulation as an obstacle to scientists, and that this is a genuine error: in her experience, scientists at the frontier of biotechnology very much want ethicists involved, very much want to know where the red lines are, so they can proceed in the confidence that society approves. She also stresses that replacing part of a rodent's brain with human brain cells raises the key question of what harm this does to the animal, especially a possible new kind of harm that you would not easily notice, and that this must be taken very seriously.

17:19 Turning a paper into an agent you can talk to
James's team at Stanford proposes turning static papers into "knowledge agents" — think of them as a paper's virtual corresponding author. Their workflow is called paper to agent: a set of AI agents reads the paper through, works out how it was done, reproduces the original results, then stores the knowledge in a server, acting as a translation layer between the human paper and any AI, so that models like ChatGPT and Claude become virtual co-authors you can ask anything about the paper, and even run analyses with your own data. James stresses this differs from simply throwing the paper into a chatbot: the latter only reads, interprets and summarises results, does not know how the results and figures were generated, and cannot use the data and code, because it has no hands-on experience; a paper agent has that hands-on experience.

item.title: The Mess in AI Evaluation Isn't a Technical Problem, It's a Transparency Problem
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-nejmaigrandrou-ai-评估的混乱不是技术问题-是透明度问题/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-nejmaigrandrou-ai-评估的混乱不是技术问题-是透明度问题/
item.description: In that 2019 systematic review, fewer than 5% of medical imaging AI papers met the rigor standards long established in other areas of medicine — and even the best-performing models only matched radiologists.
item.content:encoded:
In that 2019 systematic review, fewer than 5% of medical imaging AI papers met the rigor standards long established in other areas of medicine — and even the best-performing models only matched radiologists.

This episode is medium-density, but the first half — a first-hand account of how evidence standards in medical AI went from chaos to discipline — has direct reference value for anyone building medical AI products.

11:22 Fewer than 5% of AI papers in top journals hold up to scrutiny
Around 2019, new papers appeared every week claiming "AI is as good as radiologists" or "AI beats radiologists at pneumonia detection," yet these conclusions contradicted each other. Xiao Liu and her collaborators did something nobody was doing at the time: they took the rigor standards that the diagnostic test evaluation field had used for years and applied them to these AI papers, keeping only those with external validation, like-for-like comparisons, and meaningful control groups. The paper count collapsed — fewer than 5% actually met the standards long established in other areas of medicine. And within that small set, the best models only matched radiologists. This isn't bad news; it means the published literature contains too much noise.

16:28 Reporting guidelines don't teach you how to do research, they force you to say what you did
CONSORT, SPIRIT, PRISMA, STARD, TRIPOD — these reporting guidelines are essentially checklists specifying which items a paper must report. They don't tell you how to do the research — they're not methodology guidelines, they're transparency guidelines. Whether your methods are good or bad, you have to write them transparently and clearly. Their function is to put authors, journal editors and peer reviewers on the same information plane, with no smoke bombs and no hiding behind vague details. Xiao Liu adds a side effect: when authors know they must report a given item, it in turn forces methodological rigor upward, though that's hard to measure.

18:33 Guidelines come out of Delphi voting; items that can't reach consensus get cut
CONSORT AI and SPIRIT AI weren't written by a few people behind closed doors — they went through a Delphi process: first a literature review and expert opinion produced a set of candidate items, then multiple rounds of multi-stakeholder voting, closing with an in-person discussion. That in-person discussion is often the most valuable part, because people learn from each other. Items that can't reach consensus get excluded; only those that do are kept. Xiao Liu says doing this kind of consensus project properly takes at least six months; she tried a compressed three-month version, but participants contribute their time for free, and getting high-quality feedback and multi-round participation means you can't cut corners on time or reach.

20:36 Whether explainability belongs in reporting guidelines split the room
Andy Beam recalls that one question in the Delphi discussion was whether clinical trials should include explainability requirements, or at least report any explainability evaluation you did. He and Lauren Oakden-Rayner got up on the little stage and said "No, it shouldn't be done at all, and here's why." That argument was later commissioned as a paper by Lancet Digital Health editor Rupa, and became one of Andy's most-cited papers. In the lightning round, Xiao Liu also clearly takes the "no" side: she thinks you should first ask why you want AI explainability, and keep asking down to the bottom — what you ultimately want is just beneficial outcomes.

26:43 Advising regulators without ever working in industry felt insincere to her
At the time, Xiao Liu was doing academic AI research and clinical ophthalmology while increasingly consulting for regulators. She began to feel she had never stood on the regulated side, and that consulting was a bit insincere. So she joined Apple as a health scientist, mainly designing validation studies for wearable algorithms, such as Apple Watch sensing algorithms — including a hypertension notification feature released this year. She says Apple has a well-oiled product-shipping machine, which was exactly the experience she wanted. After more than a year there she returned to Birmingham to build a lab full-time, and then joined Microsoft AI's newly formed medical frontier LLM team.

32:49 Short term computer scientists set the direction, long term clinicians gatekeep
Asked whether medical AI will be driven more by computer scientists or clinicians, Xiao Liu first pushed back on what "driven" means, and after confirming it meant "changed," gave her judgment: short term, computer scientists and engineers; long term, clinicians. The mechanism: whoever processes the data, chooses the metrics and chooses the benchmarks determines in the short term which direction progress moves; but if the endpoint is real use on patients, clinicians will play the gatekeeper role at a later stage.

33:50 Doctors' work won't change much in five years, but should in ten
Xiao Liu thinks doctors' work won't look dramatically different within five years, but very likely will in ten and beyond — and she hopes it will. The path she envisions: if medical intelligence and models keep advancing at the current pace, the medical profession no longer has to be about accumulating knowledge, or even about the kind of medical reasoning taught in medical school; the center of gravity shifts to being "a companion to experience" — accompanying deteriorating health, sudden health events, day-to-day wellbeing fluctuations, life-changing diagnoses, treatment failures and complications, and perhaps recovery, perhaps not. She thinks people will continually need something deeply interpersonal on that journey: someone who can call on knowledge but doesn't necessarily carry it themselves, instead translating it into human language.

40:00 The most optimistic thing is dismantling old medical concepts; the most pessimistic is that we won't dare
Xiao Liu says she's more optimistic than pessimistic. What excites her most is that aggregating all the knowledge in the medical world might reveal that our understanding of biomarkers, disease phenotype clustering and existing medical knowledge frameworks is off. She gives her own PhD research on inflammatory eye diseases as an example: a pile of diseases loosely called "white dot syndromes" just because they produce white dots in the fundus, but they're very likely driven by completely different mechanisms. She hopes one way new intelligence shows up is by dismantling these old concepts in medicine. The pessimistic side: the field is inherently cautious, may resist such dismantling out of unfamiliarity, and during a period of new technological change may rigidly keep using the evaluation methods and guidelines of the past ten or twenty years, missing the chance to discover.

item.title: Government Doesn't Just Waste Your Money, It Wastes an Hour of Your Week
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-tyler-政府不只浪费你的钱-还浪费你每周一小时/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-tyler-政府不只浪费你的钱-还浪费你每周一小时/
item.description: Plenty of countries file taxes for their citizens; the IRS is legally barred from doing it for you. The time tax hits the poor, immigrants and the formerly incarcerated hardest — and AI may not save them.
item.content:encoded:
Plenty of countries file taxes for their citizens; the IRS is legally barred from doing it for you. The time tax hits the poor, immigrants and the formerly incarcerated hardest — and AI may not save them.

Medium information density, but the "time tax" frame itself is valuable: it reprices the administrative friction of the welfare state as a regressive levy. The confession in the back half about her shifting UBI stance is worth hearing.

0:58 The IRS is legally barred from filing your taxes for you
Lowrey's core example: in Japan, salaried workers never touch the tax process at all; many countries mail you a prefilled return and you only fix the errors. The US could do exactly this — nine in ten households take the standard deduction, so their tax situations are fairly simple — but the IRS is not legally permitted to. This is not a technology problem, it is an institutional choice. She defines the "time tax" as the portion of cost government shifts onto individuals as administrative labour, and unlike a monetary tax it is different in kind: you can earn more money, you cannot earn more time.

1:02 The worst program is TANF, not the IRS
Lowrey names TANF (cash welfare) the single worst program in government: it nominally exists to address child poverty, in practice it does not move the child poverty rate, its compliance burden is extremely heavy and punitive, and its $16.5 billion a year is essentially wasted. She offers a rule — programs aimed at high-income Americans are a far better experience, safety-net programs are generally bad, and welfare is the worst. This yields a counterintuitive judgment: the quality of government service is inversely proportional to the political influence of the beneficiary.

6:08 Pandemic fraud is not something the time tax can prevent
Cowen raises a common objection: fraud exploded after deregulation in 2020, so maybe the time tax is the necessary cost of fraud prevention. Lowrey rejects it outright: that fraud came mainly from criminal rings and fake small businesses, plus the fact that UI systems themselves run on ancient COBOL infrastructure. Her mechanism is misaligned incentives — governors have no incentive to upgrade UI systems when unemployment is low, so the same conversation repeats every recession. The conclusion: building state capacity and agile digital systems prevents fraud; pushing the work onto individuals does not.

11:19 Large-scale fraud is almost entirely on the supply side
Lowrey points out that Medicare and Medicaid fraud is almost entirely on the provider side: nursing homes, clinics and hospital systems defrauding the government. The ceiling on individual fraud is low, because the amount you can extract from government is limited; to commit large-scale fraud you have to process a lot of transactions. So her policy ordering is: reduce administrative overhead in other programs and concentrate enforcement resources on criminal organisations and legitimate providers, rather than loading burdens onto the 99.9% who do not commit fraud. She adds a piece of political economy: fraud narratives are often used to make programs look illegitimate, and thereby get voters to tolerate cuts.

13:25 Fifty hours per person per year, and highly unequal
Lowrey's quantitative estimate comes from the American Time Use Survey: total bureaucratic time is about 50 hours per person per year, close to an hour a week. She concedes the number is an underestimate — ATUS cannot capture multitasking (cooking while on hold is recorded as one thing), and time taxes are scattered across categories and never aggregated. Who pays the most? People entangled with the criminal justice system, immigrants, the poor. The rich can "skip" it with staff and accountants, with one exception: permits to renovate a house in San Francisco, where no amount of money spares you a 500-day wait and multiple rounds of public review.

22:57 AI can fill out forms, but it can't fill a urine test
Cowen asks whether AI agents could handle all of this within five years. Lowrey says very likely, but raises two caveats: first, the users of the most burdensome programs are low-income, and whether they know about or trust these agents is unknown; second, much of the burden is not paperwork at all — it is mandatory interviews, urine screening, data that is hard to collect. She gives SNAP as an example: benefits are calculated by household, and government has no stable definition of "household", so you have to explain how you and your co-residents split spending on staple foods — a question AI would struggle to answer for you. She notes she was originally sceptical, but a civic technologist who has worked in this field for years is convinced AI will help enormously.

31:18 Disability insurance is already hard enough to apply for
Cowen presses with data: the number of people on disability insurance rose roughly fourfold between 1990 and 2014, while workplace deaths kept falling — shouldn't the threshold be raised? Lowrey does not accept the inference. She offers two alternative explanations: population ageing and the rise in obesity-related chronic illness. Then the counter-evidence: 5% of applicants must submit more than 1,000 pages of medical material; 11,000 Americans die each year while waiting for a disability determination. She concedes she worries about both directions — about paying people who do not need it, and about denying people who genuinely do — so she does not think this is the moment to add more paperwork.

38:28 The research moved her position on UBI
Lowrey's previous book, Give People Money, was pro-UBI; here she says plainly that the research findings are "sobering" and that she has updated her priors: the side benefits she expected cash to deliver did not materialise. Her defence is that the point of giving people money is to give people money to buy things, and that rationale still holds; life improving less than expected is not an argument against the policy. On AI and UBI, she admits she was extremely dismissive of the claim that "AI will force UBI", and would not go that far now, but if GDP and productivity surge while unemployment also rises, that would be very strange, and UBI-type policies would have to be considered.

item.title: Sequoia's Former Boss on Reading People: What Happens Before 14 Sets the Core
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-ilt-红杉前掌门看人-14-岁前发生了什么-内核就定了/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-ilt-红杉前掌门看人-14-岁前发生了什么-内核就定了/
item.description: Digging into his own refugee family's history, he found that the imprint you absorb unconsciously from your parents before you are 12, 13, 14 stays with you for life; what changes afterward is the external intensity, not the core.
item.content:encoded:
Digging into his own refugee family's history, he found that the imprint you absorb unconsciously from your parents before you are 12, 13, 14 stays with you for life; what changes afterward is the external intensity, not the core.

Not an investing lesson but a retrospective on origins, reading people, and writing. The back half — on structural changes in venture capital and the great man view of history — is the most valuable; the family history up front is more personal.

7:23 The grandfather who waited for the situation to pass disappeared
Moritz's two grandfathers were two reactions to the same catastrophe. His maternal grandfather was a lower-court judge in Bavaria, had fought at Verdun in World War I, believed in the durability of the state, and had a pension he was unwilling to give up, so he delayed leaving; in the end he and his wife were sent east and vanished from history. The other grandfather was nearly blind, supported his family alone by trading cattle, had no pension to wait for, and left with his wife 72 hours before the war broke out — three days later and they too would have died. Moritz says the lesson he drew was not a moral judgment but that you must always have a bolt hole to hide in, and you can never have too many passports.

21:03 His most effective question makes people cry on the spot
When he interviews people he always asks one fixed question: looking back, if there were one thing, one action, you could have done differently, what would it be. He remembers a person interviewing at Sequoia bursting into tears when asked this — the man was the son of Latino immigrants, and at around age 12 he and a friend stole candy from a corner grocery; the owner told his father, who dragged him back to the store by the ear and made him apologize and empty his pockets. Years later, asked this question, the first thing he thought of was still the shame he had brought on his family. Moritz says many people conducting interviews are not really listening to the answer.

26:03 He sorted everyone he knew on Zoom
Inspired by a series about a French village in World War II, he divided people into three categories: resisters, the silent, and collaborators. During the pandemic, in those Zoom meetings with a dozen little windows, he would stare at each person he knew and think: if these people had lived in a French village in the 1940s, who would stay silent, who would resist, who would collaborate. He says resisters are always a tiny minority, because bad things happen in a country precisely because most people stay silent. Asked how many of the people he had invested in would be resisters, he said he would like to think so, but he is not sure.

38:04 The painter gave himself one day off a year
Frank Auerbach was a refugee from Nazi Germany, and Moritz calls him a complete monomaniac: apart from one day off each Christmas to rest at Brighton Pier, he painted every single day. His models were a small fixed group of people, the same few faces painted for decades; one model who lived in Venice flew to London once a week to sit for him. His wife's house was right on the English coast, and Moritz asked whether he went there; he answered: I have never been to that house. From this Moritz discusses the cost of monomania — the cost to relationships is almost inevitable, but sometimes great things come out of exactly there.

43:04 He bet on something beyond the résumé
Around 1985, Moritz was still a journalist and wrote to five small funds looking for a job. Everyone except Don Valentine told him he had no technical background, no engineering degree, no experience at a tech company, and suggested he go into PR or marketing. Don was willing to take the risk, for a direct reason: he had seen several people with operating backgrounds at large tech companies move into investing and fail, and he had also seen several who succeeded — an actuary, and the one he cited most, Arthur Rock: an investment banker by background, with nothing in his résumé that predicted success. Don did not believe in teaching people; he believed in throwing them into the deep end and seeing whether they drowned.

46:15 Venture capital's old advantage was imperfect information
Moritz says doing venture capital in the 1980s and '90s had several advantages that have now disappeared, the first being imperfect information: before the internet, unless you were close to something you did not know what was happening, whereas now the whole world basically gets the same information. The second is that the early market has far too many participants — individuals, two- or three-person funds, giant mutual funds — too many middlemen, and it is no longer possible for investors to build the kind of real, close relationship with founders they once had. He therefore says that a moderately intelligent, quick-witted 14- to 16-year-old could have done venture capital in the mid-'80s; he is not sure he could still do it well today.

52:57 He believes in the great man view of history without apology
Asked whether it is great individuals or enduring institutions that shape the course of history, Moritz's answer is blunt: he is a firm believer in the great man theory. From Lee Iacocca to Steve Jobs, from politics to the battlefield, what matters is great leaders; and of course also tyrants who cast a shadow over tens of millions of people for decades. In his work at Sequoia and in writing Ferguson, he cares about the same thing — how an organization stays alive across decades. And on Elon, he says he is completely stunned by the scale of his achievements across so many different industries, and thinks he may be the greatest industrialist in American history.

58:40 The more AI writes, the more valuable a human voice becomes
Moritz says that because AI can easily produce vast amounts of text, excellent writing that cuts through the garbage is actually appreciating; his definition of excellent writing is ‘a voice you can hear that cannot be mistaken for anyone else's’. The hardest thing for a writer is to get close enough to your own inner feeling and voice that it outweighs the weight of others' expectations — he quotes Joseph Campbell: the privilege of a lifetime is to become who you truly are, and that is also the hardest thing. He does not consider himself a technologist and says AI is rarely discussed at home; on employment he is optimistic: people predicted doom when the atomic bomb went off, and in the 1970s predicted a genetic revolution creating humans, and neither happened, and this time he thinks more jobs will be created than destroyed.

item.title: The strongest El Niño hasn't peaked yet, but no one alive has seen one this big
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-ologies-最强厄尔尼诺还没到峰值-但没人活着见过它这么大/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-ologies-最强厄尔尼诺还没到峰值-但没人活着见过它这么大/
item.description: The 2026 El Niño already exceeded the peaks of the two strongest events on record, 1982 and 2015, by autumn — and its peak usually doesn't arrive until winter. This is not a climate forecast for the future; it is weather that is happening now.
item.content:encoded:
The 2026 El Niño already exceeded the peaks of the two strongest events on record, 1982 and 2015, by autumn — and its peak usually doesn't arrive until winter. This is not a climate forecast for the future; it is weather that is happening now.

Meteorologist Marshall Shepherd lays out the mechanics of El Niño, how it's observed, and what it actually does — and unpacks how a UN report got misread by the media as a "strategic retreat." High information density, worth listening to.

5:24 The UN didn't say retreat — a reporter said it first
On September 2, 2026, the UN Environment Programme published a report titled "Limiting Overshoot." AP reporter Seth Borenstein wrote "strategic retreat" in the first sentence of his story, and the phrase was copied into headlines worldwide, turning into an end-of-the-world narrative of "we're done for." But the word "retreat" appears nowhere in the report; the UN was in fact doubling down on emissions cuts. What was actually abandoned was only the claim that 1.5 degrees can still be held. The report's own text says: every fraction of a degree avoided, every year of overshoot shortened, saves lives, protects ecosystems and reduces economic losses.

11:40 Climate change isn't coming to knock — it's already at the dinner table
Shepherd says the framing he grew up hearing was "climate change is coming," and that framing is now outdated. In his words, it isn't just sitting at the dinner table — it's eating dessert, the appetizer and all the main courses. He explicitly rejects any narrative that talks about climate change in the future tense: people used to discuss what 2050 or 2100 would look like, but it is already happening, and it will only get worse, because the emissions cuts that should have been made aren't really being made. He also notes that adaptation and resilience measures are increasing, because some places have realized this is bound to happen.

17:50 El Niño got its name from fishermen who caught no fish at Christmas
Every two to seven years, the Pacific trade winds weaken or even reverse, warm water in the western Pacific flows back east, and the upwelling of cold water along the South American coast shuts down. Peruvian fishermen found they caught no fish around Christmas — because the nutrients brought up by that cold water were cut off — and so the name El Niño was born. The opposite, cold phase is La Niña. Shepherd stresses this is a coupled ocean-atmosphere system, so it takes both meteorology and oceanography to understand. El Niño disturbs the upper-level jet stream through "teleconnections," spreading its effects globally; California, Georgia, the Amazon and the Sahel are all on that chain.

19:55 No hurricanes in the Atlantic, but Hawaii issued its first-ever tornado warning
El Niño suppresses Atlantic hurricane activity while strengthening the Pacific hurricane season. As of September 8, not a single hurricane had formed in the Atlantic, only a few tropical storms, and it was likely to break the record for the latest-forming hurricane since 1941. On the other side, Hawaii got the first tornado warning in the state's history because of Hurricane Lowell, with gusts on Kauai reaching 84 miles per hour. Shepherd says this is El Niño's two sets of books: the East Coast benefits while Pacific islands come under pressure. California, meanwhile, faces strong storms, rain and mudslides.

35:24 Eight degrees of warm water below the surface means there's no turning back this time
The threshold for calling an El Niño is sea surface temperatures in the central and eastern Pacific running 0.5 degrees Celsius above average, and right now they are already two to three degrees above. More critical is what lies below the surface — Shepherd cites an estimate that subsurface water temperatures are eight degrees above normal. He says this is what convinced him the 2026-2027 El Niño warming event will not fall back. World Meteorological Organization data show that by February 2027 this El Niño is almost certain to still be going strong. He stresses that he is not a scientist given to exaggeration, but this may be the strongest El Niño that anyone alive on Earth has ever seen.

38:33 Weather is mood, climate is personality
Shepherd uses this metaphor to explain why every El Niño is different — they have their own "personalities," but the West Coast's average personality is heavy rain and natural disasters like landslides and mudslides. His concrete advice is an "El Niño plan": know where your important documents are, know what extreme weather your area tends to get under El Niño, and know which National Weather Service office covers you — Los Angeles, San Francisco and Sacramento each have their own office issuing warnings. He also mentions the nighttime tornadoes common in the Southeast, and suggests people make checking the weather before bed a habit, like brushing their teeth.

49:17 Teleconnections: how a pool of warm water in the Pacific changes global weather
Shepherd explains that the mechanism by which El Niño affects the globe is called "teleconnection." A large pool of warm water in the central and eastern Pacific alters the atmospheric column above it, disturbing the upper-level jet stream. He uses the analogy of ripples in a pond: drop a few sticks or a stone in the middle of the ripples and they get scrambled. The disturbance El Niño creates propagates through the atmosphere via teleconnection patterns, carrying weather changes around the world. He also stresses that it is precisely because fluid dynamics is governed by physical equations — the Navier-Stokes equations, thermodynamic equations, the continuity equation — that weather is predictable to some degree; forecasting is essentially predicting how this fluid will flow.

56:37 After El Niño comes a fiercer fire season
Shepherd points out that the problem with extreme weather is that "both sets of books go wrong" — it isn't just drier or just wetter, it's both. El Niño brings rain, storms and mudslides to the western US, but it also makes vegetation grow heavily; a year or two later, when the climate turns dry, that vegetation becomes fuel and amplifies fire season. He calls this a Jekyll and Hyde, dual-personality effect, and says it's why he has devoted so much attention to studying the western US. He also mentions that his colleague Kim Cobb has studied whether El Niño is becoming stronger or more frequent because of climate change, and believes a link is likely.

item.title: A Math Professor and NFL Player Who Says He Was Just Lucky
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-freakonomics-数学教授和nfl球员-他说自己只是运气好/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-freakonomics-数学教授和nfl球员-他说自己只是运气好/
item.description: John Urschel played in the NFL while finishing an MIT math PhD, yet says talent is only a small part of it — his success came from "an enormous amount of hard work" and luck. He even hopes his football fame did not get him his MIT job.
item.content:encoded:
John Urschel played in the NFL while finishing an MIT math PhD, yet says talent is only a small part of it — his success came from "an enormous amount of hard work" and luck. He even hopes his football fame did not get him his MIT job.

This is the audio version of a video interview, so the information density is not high, but Urschel on how he crammed two full-time jobs into the same week, and why he ultimately quit football, is worth hearing.

8:16 A coach's joke made him realize he could make the NFL
After Urschel's junior season, his position coach pulled him aside, essentially saying "don't go thinking about anything crazy, stay another year" — the crazy thing being declaring early for the draft. He hadn't been thinking about the NFL at all, but that remark made him realize for the first time: this would happen if he wanted it. Later the coach would say in practice, "they [the league] will like this move." He wasn't running on self-confidence; he was running on other people assuming he belonged at that level.

13:25 He asked his coach about a PhD; the coach thought he already had one
Urschel was doing an MIT math PhD while playing in the NFL, and he says he "didn't cheat," because he asked coach John Harbaugh in advance whether he could go back to school for a degree. The coach replied "absolutely, we support players finishing their education," then a minute later added a text: "I thought you already had a degree and a master's." Urschel replied: "But I don't have a PhD." The coach replied "oh, OK," and that was the approval. He deliberately picked courses with no exams that he could pass by reading the textbook — three PhD courses in one semester.

15:35 On planes he pretended his math book was a chess book
During the NFL season almost all his time each day went to football, with film study at night. Math could only be done in the time other people used to relax — say, on the team flight, when everyone was watching movies. He says reading a chess book would have been completely fine, but reading a math book was "a little suspicious," and teammates might think he was too distracted, so he would say "it's not a math book, it's a chess book," flip it open for them, and they'd say "OK." The real solution was that he finished the textbook before the semester even started — otherwise it would have been impossible.

17:42 The CTE controversy conveniently gave him cover to retire
The host asked whether the years when CTE (brain damage from repeated head hits) was making NFL headlines happened to coincide with his considering retirement. Urschel said "it gave me great cover." But he also says he was worried before that. He was weighing whether to play another season — the last year of his rookie contract, with the next contract worth at least a million dollars a year, while his first-year base salary was 420,000. He had at one point convinced himself to stay with "there's one year left on the contract, I'll honor it" — the same mindset as when he honored his commitment to Penn State.

19:49 Looking back, he doesn't know what he was agonizing over
Urschel says looking back, agonizing over retirement made no sense: the team could cut him at any time, the contract wasn't guaranteed, and an injury would end it. What he actually cared about was math and his newborn child, and both were growing more important, while football ranked third yet was a real burden on the first two — not just his head, but his whole body, whether he'd still be able to walk at 50, to pick up his grandchildren and his daughter. He says "I needed to retire, focus on math, and go be with my kid."

20:52 He estimates only 4% of Americans like math
The host asked him to guess how many out of 100 Americans like math, and Urschel said that if you define "math" the way the general public understands it, 4% might even be high. The host said that number was a little sad in how low it was. Urschel's own definition is very broad: math is the quantitative language we all share for reasoning about problems, and engineering, theoretical physics, statistics and theoretical computer science all count as math — not far from doing puzzles, not far from the goal of "understanding something."

27:07 His daughter won't play football; his son has to really need it
Asked whether his two children should play football, Urschel said his daughter shouldn't — that level of risk he won't accept. For his son, if it looks like something he "really needs to do," he would allow it. He explains what needing means: football suits young people who have that craving and can benefit from "consensual violence, controlled, agreed-upon aggression" — with rules, not trying to hurt people, essentially a proxy for war. He says it was very good for the combative high schooler he once was. If it's just "because Dad played" or "because all my friends play," he'd have the kid try wrestling or judo first.

29:09 He says he actually had no talent as an NFL player
The host praised him for being good at several hard things at once, and Urschel said talent does play a role, but compared with NFL players he "had no talent" — he concedes he has some athletic gifts, like broad shoulders, but in the league that doesn't count. So how did he succeed? "Hard work, an enormous amount of hard work." The source is "wanting to be better." Asked whether his MIT job came from his football fame, he said "I don't know, I hope not."

item.title: Bypassing CUDA for inference chips is inevitable, but SRAM's window may not stay open forever
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-sv101-推理芯片绕过cuda是必然-但sram的窗口未必一直开着/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-sv101-推理芯片绕过cuda是必然-但sram的窗口未必一直开着/
item.description: Training is about compute, inference is about bandwidth. Groq and Cerebras both bet on SRAM, but one discounts for determinism and the other for yield. OpenAI chose the most expensive HBM4 because what it lacks is power, not money.
item.content:encoded:
Training is about compute, inference is about bandwidth. Groq and Cerebras both bet on SRAM, but one discounts for determinism and the other for yield. OpenAI chose the most expensive HBM4 because what it lacks is power, not money.

Two frontline chip entrepreneurs break down the trade-offs of Groq, Cerebras, and OpenAI's three paths, with plenty of engineering details and cost accounting. For anyone trying to understand what inference chips are really betting on.

4:17 Training bets on compute, inference bets on bandwidth
In the training era, no one could make money from training itself, so costs couldn't be quantified; everyone just wanted to bet on the strongest cluster. In the inference era, the math is clear: how much does the user pay per million tokens, and how much does it cost me to produce those million tokens.
